case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a court of appeals must review de novo (rather than for substantial evidence) the agency’s determination that an asylum applicant’s harms do not rise to the level of “persecution.”
case_analysis.legal_provision: 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(42)(A) (definition of “refugee,” incorporating the “persecution” standard) and the INA’s judicial-review framework requiring substantial-evidence review of agency factfinding (commonly applied via 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B)).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that the agency’s conclusion that the threats and physical mistreatment described in the record are not “persecution” is not a purely factual finding but a mixed question (application of a legal standard to established facts) that should receive more searching judicial review than deferential substantial-evidence review. They contend that treating “persecution” as a fact question enables inconsistent outcomes and insulates legal error, particularly given systemic issues in immigration adjudication (including summary affirmances and high-volume decisionmaking), and that appellate courts should independently assess whether the proved harms legally qualify as persecution under the statute.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent argues that the court of appeals correctly applied the INA’s substantial-evidence standard because the agency determination that particular harms do or do not amount to “persecution” is a fact-bound assessment committed to the immigration courts and the BIA. The government characterizes the issue as turning on record-specific line-drawing rather than a pure legal rule, emphasizes Congress’s choice of deferential review to promote efficiency and uniformity, and maintains that the First Circuit properly upheld the agency’s finding that petitioners’ alleged threats and mistreatment in El Salvador did not compel a conclusion of persecution under 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(42)(A).
key_precedents: Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369 (2024)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to insist that meaningful review must remain for genuine legal error—particularly if the agency effectively ratchets up the persecution threshold or refuses to consider cumulative harm. But, as Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 1252(b)(4)(B) directly prescribes a deferential posture for the agency’s record-bound determination unless the evidence compels the contrary conclusion, while leaving courts free to correct misstatements of the legal standard itself. The way to meet Sotomayor’s concern is to police whether the IJ/BIA articulated and applied the correct legal framework, not to relabel a disagreement over degree and severity as de novo “law” review. On this record, the First Circuit applied substantial-evidence review without insulating legal error, and we should not rewrite Congress’s review scheme.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to warn that an agency can smuggle legal error into a persecution determination by ratcheting up the standard or ignoring cumulative harm, and courts must remain able to correct those mistakes. But where (as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett emphasize) the agency articulated the correct legal framework, § 1252(b)(4)(B) supplies the governing posture: the agency’s record-bound determination is conclusive unless the evidence compels the opposite result. Petitioners’ approach would invite routine relabeling of disagreements over degree and severity as “law,” effectively rewriting Congress’s chosen standard into de novo review. On this record, the challenge is chiefly to the agency’s line-drawing, not to an identifiable misdefinition or categorical legal rule, so substantial-evidence review controls and the First Circuit’s approach fits the statute’s structure.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to worry that calling the persecution determination a “fact” could, in some cases, obscure a legal mistake—particularly if the agency effectively adopts an impermissibly heightened threshold or refuses to consider cumulative harm. But that concern is addressed, as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan explain, by preserving de novo review over the governing legal standard while applying § 1252(b)(4)(B)’s command of deference to the agency’s record-bound line-drawing unless the evidence compels the opposite conclusion. The INA’s design—layered administrative decisionmaking culminating in IJ and BIA review—confirms Congress meant courts to correct legal misdefinitions, not to reweigh severity and degree under a de novo label. On this record, the First Circuit applied the substantial-evidence framework without foreclosing legal-error review, so I see no statutory basis to adopt petitioners’ broader de novo approach.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I accept Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Barrett’s core point that § 1252(b)(4)(B) forecloses appellate reweighing of “brute” facts—credibility, frequency, severity—absent a record that compels the contrary. But the critical danger they understate is that an agency can entrench an impermissibly demanding persecution threshold (or fail to aggregate harms in substance, not merely in words) while reciting the “right” legal test, and then insulate that error by labeling the ultimate characterization as a factual finding. Meaningful judicial review—grounded in the INA’s structure and the constitutional floor reflected in habeas and due process traditions—requires courts to review de novo whether the agency’s characterization reflects the correct legal yardstick, especially where the underlying facts are essentially settled and the dispute is about the governing standard’s application. On this record, petitioners plausibly allege a misapprehension of what the law counts as persecution in the aggregate, not just a request to relitigate degree, so I would not treat § 1252(b)(4)(B) as an all-purpose shield for legal misclassification.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to worry that calling a persecution determination “fact” could, in practice, shield legal error—especially if the agency smuggles in a heightened threshold or refuses to consider cumulative harm. But the way to meet that concern is not to relabel the whole inquiry de novo; it is to preserve full judicial correction of legal misstatements while respecting § 1252(b)(4)(B)’s directive that record-bound line-drawing is conclusive unless the evidence compels the opposite result, as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett emphasize. As in my prior APA-related writing, “independent judgment” about what the law requires can coexist with a deferential standard for applying that law to a particular record when Congress has prescribed one. On this record, petitioners’ challenge looks like disagreement with degree and characterization under an accepted legal framework, so substantial-evidence review is the statutory fit.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to insist that courts must correct genuine legal error—like an agency rule that discounts cumulative harm or demands a near-fatal threshold before "persecution" can be found. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett explain, § 1252(b)(4)(B) speaks in mandatory terms: once the agency states the correct legal standard, its record-bound line-drawing about whether these particular harms cross the persecution line is “conclusive” unless a reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to find otherwise. Recasting that disagreement as “legal characterization” would, in practice, flip Congress’s chosen standard and invite appellate reweighing of severity and context—work the INA assigns to the IJ and BIA in the first instance. On this record, the agency’s view remains among “potentially many reasonable possibilities,” so substantial-evidence review—and affirmance—follows.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to warn that calling something “not persecution” can sometimes conceal a legal error—such as ignoring cumulative harm or silently imposing an impermissibly high threshold—and courts must review the legal meaning of “persecution” de novo. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, once the agency articulates the correct legal framework, § 1252(b)(4)(B) directs that the agency’s record-bound line-drawing is conclusive unless the evidence compels the contrary conclusion. Petitioners’ argument here, as framed, primarily seeks appellate reweighing of severity and degree rather than identifying a misstatement of the governing legal standard, so grafting de novo review onto that application would dilute Congress’s chosen review scheme. The proper safeguard for Sotomayor’s concern is to police for true legal misdefinition or refusal to consider cumulation, not to relabel ordinary case-specific characterization disputes as “law.”

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to worry that calling the persecution determination “fact” could conceal a legal mistake—like imposing an impermissibly high severity threshold or ignoring cumulative harm. But § 1252(b)(4)(B) speaks in mandatory terms about the review posture for “administrative findings of fact,” and as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, courts can still review de novo the legal meaning of “persecution” and police whether the agency applied the correct framework (including cumulation). What petitioners seek here is effectively de novo reclassification of a record-bound severity line-drawing; treating that as a “question of law” would dilute Congress’s chosen substantial-evidence regime and invite appellate reweighing. Absent a demonstrated misstatement of the governing standard, the statute instructs us to uphold the agency unless the record compels the contrary conclusion.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to warn that calling a persecution determination “fact” can, in practice, conceal a legal mistake—especially if the agency silently demands an impermissibly high severity threshold or refuses to aggregate harms. But the INA’s text sets out the fix for that problem: courts may correct misstatements of the governing legal standard, while § 1252(b)(4)(B) directs that record-bound findings remain “conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled” to reach the opposite result. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, de novo review properly applies to the legal meaning of “persecution,” yet this case turns on severity, frequency, and cumulative impact—quintessential line-drawing that Congress placed under substantial-evidence review. Because petitioners’ challenge largely seeks appellate reweighing of this record rather than identifying a clear legal-rule distortion, I do not see a basis to depart from the First Circuit’s compelled-to-conclude posture.

John Roberts.reasoning: The governing framework here is Congress’s choice in the INA to make “administrative findings of fact … conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary,” 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B), and our cases instruct that courts may not reweigh record facts under a more searching standard simply by relabeling a record-bound determination as “law.” Whether the particular threats and physical mistreatment shown in this record cross the line into “persecution” is a fact-intensive, context-dependent judgment—one that turns on degree, severity, and cumulative effect—and the court of appeals properly asked only whether the evidence compelled the opposite conclusion, rather than substituting its own view of the line. De novo review remains appropriate for the legal meaning of “persecution” as a statutory term, but once the agency applies that meaning to the settled historical facts, the INA’s deferential review standard controls absent a legal error in the agency’s articulation of the governing rule. On these facts, the First Circuit’s substantial-evidence affirmance respected the statute’s allocation of responsibility to the agency factfinder and stayed within the limits of judicial review.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The INA’s judicial-review scheme makes Congress’s chosen standards of review controlling, and § 1252(b)(4)(B) directs courts to treat the agency’s “findings of fact” as “conclusive” unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to reach the opposite conclusion. The determination whether the particular threats and physical mistreatment described in this record rise to the level of “persecution” is a quintessentially fact-bound line-drawing judgment about the severity of harm, and petitioners’ request for de novo review would expand the statute’s narrow allowance for judicial correction of legal error beyond its text. Reading the INA’s review provisions as a coherent whole, the better view is that courts should correct only genuine legal mistakes (e.g., use of an incorrect legal definition of “persecution”), but otherwise apply deferential substantial-evidence review to the agency’s application of that standard to the facts found. On this record, the First Circuit properly asked only whether the evidence compelled a finding of persecution and concluded it did not.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The INA’s judicial-review architecture draws a sharp line between agency factfinding and appellate reweighing of the record: under 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B), “administrative findings of fact are conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary.” Here, the agency’s determination that the petitioners’ threats and physical mistreatment in El Salvador did not rise to the level of “persecution” is a quintessentially fact-bound, record-specific line-drawing judgment committed in the first instance to the IJ and the BIA within the multi-level administrative process Congress designed. Congress codified in § 1252(b)(4)(B) the very substantial-evidence formulation this Court used in INS v. Elias-Zacarias, and nothing in the INA’s text suggests that courts of appeals must conduct a de novo reclassification of a given set of harms as “persecution,” particularly where doing so would invite systemic relitigation of intensely granular disputes and undermine the efficiency Congress sought. On this record, the First Circuit properly asked whether the evidence compelled a contrary conclusion, not whether it would have characterized the harms differently in the first instance.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The INA’s review scheme must preserve a meaningful avenue for judicial review of legal error, and a determination that undisputed threats and physical mistreatment do not amount to “persecution” is not merely a contest over “brute facts” but an application of a statutory standard to established facts. Treating that application as effectively unreviewable under substantial-evidence review risks insulating misapprehensions of the governing legal standard (e.g., minimizing cumulative harm or improperly demanding severe injury) and invites inconsistent, unreasoned outcomes in high-volume adjudication. Under this Court’s mixed-question framework, whether the proved harms satisfy the legal threshold of “persecution” is the kind of inquiry that requires elaborating a broad legal standard and developing auxiliary principles, warranting de novo review at least as to the legal characterization and standard applied. Because petitioners allege the agency legally misclassified their record-described harms as non-persecutory, the court of appeals should have independently assessed that legal conclusion rather than deferring as if it were pure factfinding.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The INA’s review scheme is the starting point: § 1252(b)(4)(B) directs courts of appeals to treat “administrative findings of fact” as “conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary,” which is substantial-evidence review, not de novo. Petitioners ask us to infer a different, more searching standard from the statute’s silence about “persecution” determinations, but—as in my prior writing on review standards—general language about courts “decid[ing]” legal questions does not itself prescribe de novo review, and a court can exercise independent judgment while still respecting Congress’s chosen deference where the determination is fact-intensive line-drawing. On this record, the agency’s conclusion that the threats and mistreatment in El Salvador did not rise to the level of persecution is the kind of application-of-standard-to-facts assessment Congress typically leaves primarily to the immigration adjudicators, subject to substantial-evidence backstop rather than judicial reweighing. Courts remain free to correct legal errors about what “persecution” means, but where (as here) the dispute is whether these particular harms cross the statutory threshold, § 1252(b)(4)(B) supplies the operative posture.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The INA instructs that “administrative findings of fact are conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary,” § 1252(b)(4)(B), and the question whether the threats and physical mistreatment shown in this record cross the line into “persecution” is a paradigmatically fact-bound application of a general statutory standard to case-specific circumstances. Whatever one might think of a different line, our task is not to reweigh the evidence or impose a judge-made de novo overlay that would “flip” Congress’s chosen standard of review; we ask only whether a reasonable factfinder could agree with the IJ/BIA that these harms, as found, did not amount to persecution. On this record, the agency’s view is at least one of “potentially many reasonable possibilities,” so the court of appeals properly applied substantial-evidence review and affirmed. Petitioners remain free to argue legal error about the definition of “persecution,” but they cannot recast disagreement with the agency’s fact-bound line-drawing as entitlement to de novo review.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The INA’s judicial-review framework directs courts of appeals to treat the agency’s “findings of fact” as “conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary,” 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B). Here, the BIA’s determination that petitioners’ record-described threats and physical mistreatment in El Salvador did not rise to the level of “persecution” is a highly fact-bound, line-drawing application of the governing standard to the particular circumstances, and Congress’s text channels that kind of case-specific assessment into substantial-evidence review rather than de novo reconsideration. Courts remain free to independently determine the legal meaning of “persecution” under § 1101(a)(42)(A), but once the legal standard is correctly identified, whether this record compels a finding that the harms meet that threshold is reviewed deferentially—and the First Circuit properly asked whether the evidence compelled the contrary conclusion. Petitioners’ policy concerns about inconsistency cannot overcome the statute’s chosen standard of review for agency adjudicative determinations in removal cases.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The INA’s judicial-review framework directs that “administrative findings of fact are conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary,” § 1252(b)(4)(B), and the agency’s determination that the particular threats and mistreatment in this record do not rise to the level of “persecution” is a predominantly fact-bound line-drawing judgment about degree and severity. Read in statutory context, Congress paired the refugee definition in § 1101(a)(42)(A) with a deferential review regime for agency factfinding, and nothing in the text carves out a de novo rule for this kind of record-specific application. Petitioners’ reliance on mixed-question cases like Guerrero-Lasprilla is misplaced because those decisions construed “questions of law” in a jurisdictional savings clause and expressly did not decide the standard of review; where § 1252(b)(4)(B) speaks directly, the plain meaning of that provision—not interpretive presumptions—controls. On these facts, the First Circuit properly asked whether the record compelled a contrary conclusion and upheld the agency’s determination under substantial-evidence review.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The INA’s judicial-review text directs that “administrative findings of fact are conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary,” 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B), and in context that substantial-evidence rule reaches determinations that are at most mixed questions whose resolution is “primarily … factual.” Applying this Court’s mixed-question framework, the agency’s conclusion that the record-described threats and physical mistreatment in El Salvador did not cross the line into “persecution” turns on weighing severity, frequency, and cumulative impact—work that is intensely fact-bound and best performed by the IJ/BIA rather than an appellate court reappraising the record de novo. Nothing in § 1101(a)(42)(A)’s incorporation of “persecution” suggests Congress displaced that deferential review scheme for this category of line-drawing, and petitioners’ uniformity concerns cannot override the statute’s review allocation. Under § 1252(b)(4)(B), the court of appeals properly asked only whether the evidence compelled a contrary conclusion, not whether it would have labeled the harms “persecution” in the first instance.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a court of appeals must review de novo (rather than for substantial evidence) the agency’s determination that an asylum applicant’s threats and physical mistreatment did not amount to “persecution.”
case_analysis.legal_provision: 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(42)(A) (definition of “refugee,” incorporating the persecution standard for asylum eligibility), as applied through the INA’s judicial-review framework (including the substantial-evidence standard for agency factfinding).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that whether a given set of established facts rises to the legal level of “persecution” is a mixed question of law and fact that should receive de novo appellate review (or at least more searching review than substantial-evidence). They contend that treating the persecution determination as effectively factual and deferring to the BIA/IJ under substantial-evidence review entrenches inconsistency across cases, permits under-enforcement of the statutory protection for refugees, and is especially problematic given the BIA’s streamlined/summary decision practices and the high stakes of removal to danger.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The government argues that the First Circuit correctly applied the INA’s substantial-evidence standard because the persecution inquiry here is a fact-bound application of law to the specific record, not a pure legal question. It maintains that Congress chose deferential review to promote efficiency and uniformity in the immigration system, and that the agency’s finding that the alleged threats and mistreatment did not rise to persecution was supported by substantial evidence on this record, so the court of appeals properly affirmed.
key_precedents: Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369 (2024)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to insist that genuine legal errors—misdefining “persecution” or adopting an impermissible categorical rule—remain reviewable and correctable, and our opinion should make that explicit. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Thomas underscore, Guerrero-Lasprilla and Wilkinson address what is reviewable as a jurisdictional matter; they do not displace Congress’s separate, categorical instruction in § 1252(b)(4)(B) that record-bound, degree-and-context determinations are conclusive unless the evidence compels the opposite result. Here, the agency articulated the correct legal standard and explained its assessment; petitioners’ theory would invite courts to relabel disagreement with that application as “law” and thereby reweigh severity and context de novo, which § 1252(b)(4)(B) forecloses. A narrower holding—de novo review for definitional or categorical legal mistakes, but substantial-evidence review for this fact-intensive persecution line-drawing—best fits the statute and should hold the coalition.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is her antecedent “classification” argument: that the ultimate persecution determination is a mixed question and therefore a “question of law” under Guerrero-Lasprilla and Wilkinson. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, those cases speak to what is reviewable as a jurisdictional matter under § 1252(a)(2)(D); they do not displace Congress’s separate, categorical instruction in § 1252(b)(4)(B) that administrative factfinding is conclusive unless the record compels the contrary. Where the agency applied the undisputed legal yardstick and made a record-bound severity and context judgment, relabeling that disagreement as “law” would effectively convert substantial-evidence review into de novo reweighing—precisely what § 1252(b)(4)(B) forecloses in IIRIRA’s restrictive review scheme.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is her “classification” argument: that the ultimate persecution determination is a mixed question and thus a “question of law” under Guerrero-Lasprilla and Wilkinson. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, those cases address what is reviewable under § 1252(a)(2)(D), not the distinct instruction in § 1252(b)(4)(B) that administrative factfinding is conclusive absent a record-compelled contrary result; nothing in the INA suggests that Congress meant courts to perform de novo reassessments of record-bound severity line-drawing simply by relabeling it “legal.” Here, the agency repeatedly articulated the correct persecution standard and gave a record-specific explanation; petitioners’ challenge, like Justice Barrett notes, is functionally a request to reweigh degree, frequency, and consequences. On this record, the evidence does not compel the opposite conclusion, so substantial-evidence review controls and the denial must be upheld.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Chief Justice is right that § 1252(b)(4)(B) commands substantial-evidence deference for “administrative findings of fact,” and I do not read Guerrero-Lasprilla or Wilkinson to authorize courts to reweigh what occurred or how severe it was. But Roberts’ and Justice Kagan’s framing still skips the antecedent classification problem: whether the agency’s bottom-line determination that the facts found do not meet the statutory threshold of “persecution” is itself a “finding of fact,” or instead the application of a legal standard to established facts—i.e., a mixed question that remains reviewable as a “question of law” under § 1252(a)(2)(D). Treating that characterization as purely factual, as Justice Thomas urges, risks insulating legal drift in the governing standard by allowing the agency to ratchet the persecution threshold without meaningful judicial checking for correctness “under governing law,” especially where the alleged error is the yardstick’s calibration rather than evidentiary support. The proper approach is bifurcated: defer under § 1252(b)(4)(B) to historical factfinding unless the record compels otherwise, but review independently whether those facts, as found, satisfy the legal standard for persecution and whether the agency applied an impermissibly demanding rule in substance.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right that calling something “mixed” does not settle the standard of review, and Guerrero-Lasprilla/Wilkinson confirm that mixed questions can be “questions of law” for jurisdictional purposes. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett emphasize, that jurisdictional label does not override Congress’s separate, explicit review instruction in § 1252(b)(4)(B): record-bound determinations are conclusive unless the evidence compels the contrary. The ultimate persecution call here—whether a particular course of threats and mistreatment crosses a severity threshold—is exactly the kind of degree-and-context judgment that functions like factfinding in operation, so independent judicial review properly occurs through substantial-evidence review (plus correction of genuine legal errors), not de novo reweighing. Petitioners’ approach risks collapsing § 1252(b)(4)(B) by inviting courts to relabel routine disagreements with the agency’s severity assessment as “law” and retry asylum records on appeal.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to insist that courts must correct genuine legal errors—misdefining “persecution” or applying an impermissible categorical rule—and Guerrero-Lasprilla/Wilkinson confirm mixed questions can be reviewable as “questions of law” for jurisdictional purposes. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, that jurisdictional label does not displace Congress’s separate, categorical instruction in § 1252(b)(4)(B) that administrative factfinding is conclusive unless the record compels the contrary. The persecution line here is a degree-and-context judgment—severity, repetition, consequences—that operates like factfinding, so turning it into de novo review would invite the very reweighing of records Congress foreclosed. Applying Chenery/Bowman, we ask whether the agency applied the correct yardstick and whether its path is reasonably discernible; on this record the contrary conclusion is not compelled.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: I agree with the Chief Justice, Justice Kagan, and Justice Thomas that § 1252(b)(4)(B) imposes a highly deferential substantial-evidence constraint on the agency’s historical factfinding and that courts may not reweigh severity, frequency, and context as fact questions. But that does not resolve the antecedent classification issue: whether the agency’s ultimate determination that the found facts do not meet the statutory threshold of “persecution” is itself an “administrative finding of fact” within § 1252(b)(4)(B), or instead a predominantly legal application of the statutory standard that requires independent judicial judgment to keep the legal yardstick uniform across cases. Justice Roberts is right that petitioners cannot manufacture de novo review by relabeling mere disagreement as “law,” yet my concern remains that treating the bottom-line persecution threshold as conclusive factfinding effectively expands § 1252(b)(4)(B) beyond its terms and risks insulating legal drift absent a clear congressional command. I would reverse and remand for de novo review of the persecution characterization (with appropriate respect to the agency) while maintaining compelled-to-conclude deference for the underlying factual findings.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kavanaugh are right that Guerrero-Lasprilla and Wilkinson treat some mixed questions as “questions of law” for § 1252(a)(2)(D)’s jurisdictional gatekeeping, and that courts must correct genuine legal mistakes about the governing yardstick. But that does not answer the separate, textually specific standard-of-review directive in § 1252(b)(4)(B), which makes the agency’s fact-bound, degree-and-context judgments conclusive unless the record compels a contrary conclusion. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, the disagreement here is not about the legal meaning of “persecution” or an impermissible categorical rule; it is about whether this record’s threats and mistreatment cross the severity threshold, which operates like a factual finding under Congress’s scheme. So de novo review remains for misstatements of the standard, but petitioners’ framing would effectively invite appellate reweighing that § 1252(b)(4)(B) forbids.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kavanaugh are right to insist that the application of a legal standard to found facts can qualify as a “question of law” under Guerrero-Lasprilla and Wilkinson, and that courts must correct genuine legal errors (misdefinition of “persecution,” categorical rules, or an unlawfully heightened standard). But that jurisdictional point does not resolve the distinct, textually specified standard-of-review question Congress answered in § 1252(b)(4)(B): when the agency applies the correct yardstick and the dispute is whether this record’s threats and mistreatment cross a severity line, the inquiry operates as a record-bound determination that must be upheld unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude otherwise. As Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice emphasize, petitioners’ framing risks converting substantial-evidence review into de novo reweighing whenever a court relabels a fact-intensive severity assessment as “legal characterization.” De novo review remains available for true legal mistakes, but on this record the challenge is primarily to the agency’s degree-and-context assessment, which § 1252(b)(4)(B) channels into deferential review.

John Roberts.reasoning: The threshold question is the governing standard of review Congress prescribed in the INA: 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B) directs that “administrative findings of fact are conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary,” a substantial-evidence constraint that bars a court of appeals from reweighing a fact-bound record simply because it would label the threats and mistreatment “persecution” in the first instance. On this record, the agency’s determination that the alleged threats and physical mistreatment did not rise to the level of persecution is the kind of case-specific application of a general standard that Congress committed primarily to the agency, and judicial review remains narrow—asking whether the agency’s conclusion is supported by reasonable, substantial, and probative evidence, not whether it is the best view. Petitioners’ call for de novo review would effectively convert the reviewing court into the primary decisionmaker on the operative factual inferences (severity, frequency, and consequences of harm), contrary to the statute’s deferential framework and this Court’s repeated instruction that courts may not conduct a “de novo inquiry” into asylum eligibility. Because the evidence does not compel the opposite conclusion, the court of appeals properly affirmed under substantial-evidence review.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The INA’s judicial-review scheme directs courts of appeals to treat “administrative findings of fact” as “conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary,” 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B), and nothing in that text suggests a de novo carveout for the agency’s record-bound determination that the threats and physical mistreatment here did not rise to the requisite severity. Whether these particular incidents amount to “persecution” is, at most, a mixed question that is predominantly factual because it turns on degree, context, and the intensity of harm shown in the record; absent clear textual warrant, “questions of law” cannot be expanded to reclassify such fact-laden applications as de novo issues. Guerrero-Lasprilla and Wilkinson addressed jurisdiction under § 1252(a)(2)(D), not the standard of review mandated by § 1252(b)(4)(B), and in any event Congress gave clear and convincing evidence of its intent to channel and narrow review through deferential fact review even if that reduces “meaningful” judicial oversight. On this record, where the IJ/BIA found the mistreatment insufficiently severe, the court of appeals properly applied substantial-evidence review rather than substituting its own judgment de novo.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The INA’s judicial-review provision draws a sharp line: “administrative findings of fact are conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary.” 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B). On this record, the agency’s determination that the applicant’s threats and physical mistreatment did not rise to the level of “persecution” is a fact-bound application of the statutory standard to particular events, and nothing in the INA’s interlocking provisions specifies de novo review by courts of appeals for that determination. Consistent with the statute-centered review scheme Congress chose, the court of appeals properly applied substantial-evidence review and affirmed because the record did not compel the opposite conclusion. Petitioners’ request to reclassify this assessment as de novo review would effectively override § 1252(b)(4)(B)’s prescribed deference for agency determinations grounded in the evidentiary record.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The question whether the threats and physical mistreatment found (or assumed) by the IJ/BIA rise to the statutory level of “persecution” is a classic mixed question—applying a legal standard to established facts—so it is properly treated as a “question[] of law” within the INA’s review framework. Under Guerrero-Lasprilla, as reaffirmed in Wilkinson, courts of appeals must retain de novo authority to decide that legal application, while still reviewing the agency’s underlying historical factfinding (what happened, credibility, severity, frequency) only for substantial evidence under § 1252(b)(4)(B). Treating the persecution determination as effectively factual would insulate whether the agency applied the correct legal yardstick, risking arbitrary or legally erroneous denials that Congress did not make “functionally unreviewable.” Because petitioners’ challenge is to the legal characterization of the mistreatment as non-persecutory—not merely a request to reweigh evidence—the court of appeals should not have applied only substantial-evidence deference to that ultimate persecution determination.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The INA’s review provision, 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B), directs courts to treat “administrative findings of fact” as “conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary,” and nothing in the text or structure clearly reclassifies the highly record-bound “persecution” determination into a de novo question. As in my approach to APA § 706, “independent judgment” does not inherently require de novo review; courts can (and traditionally do) exercise independent review while applying a deferential substantial-evidence standard to predominantly factual applications of law to a particular record—like evaluating the severity, frequency, and context of threats and mistreatment. Guerrero-Lasprilla’s holding that “questions of law” include mixed questions for jurisdictional purposes does not answer the separate standard-of-review question, and historical practice in asylum cases (including this Court’s treatment in Elias-Zacarias) supports substantial-evidence review of fact-intensive eligibility determinations. On these facts—threats and physical mistreatment assessed by the IJ/BIA as not crossing the persecution line—the court of appeals properly asked whether the record compelled the opposite conclusion, not whether it would reach that conclusion anew.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Under the INA, “administrative findings of fact are conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary,” and the agency’s determination that the applicant’s particular threats and physical mistreatment did not cross the line into “persecution” is the kind of case-specific, circumstance-bound judgment that is primarily factual in operation. A court of appeals exceeds its proper role when it reweighs the evidence and substitutes its own view of how severe the mistreatment was, rather than asking the only question Congress assigned it: whether any reasonable adjudicator could have reached the agency’s conclusion on this record. Applying Chenery and Bowman, we review the reasons the IJ/BIA actually gave and will not demand “magic words” so long as the agency’s path is reasonably discernible; here, the agency plausibly explained why the incidents, considered in context, did not rise to persecution. Because the record does not compel the contrary conclusion, substantial-evidence review governs and the agency’s determination should be affirmed.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The INA’s judicial-review framework draws a key line between agency factfinding, which is reviewed under § 1252(b)(4)(B)’s substantial-evidence standard, and the legal meaning of statutory terms, which courts must determine independently using ordinary tools of statutory interpretation (with appropriate respect to the agency). Here, the underlying events—what threats were made, what physical mistreatment occurred, and their frequency and severity—are factual issues subject to substantial-evidence deference; but whether those established facts meet the statutory standard of “persecution” under § 1101(a)(42)(A) is a legal characterization (a mixed question with a predominantly legal component) requiring de novo review. Treating the persecution threshold as effectively a fact question would improperly collapse legal interpretation into fact review and would extend deference beyond what Congress prescribed. Because the court of appeals should have independently assessed whether the found threats and mistreatment, taken together, satisfy the legal standard of persecution, I would vote to reverse and remand for de novo review of that legal determination.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The INA directs courts of appeals to treat the agency’s “administrative findings of fact” as “conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary.” 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B). On this record—where the asylum applicant alleges threats and physical mistreatment—the agency’s bottom-line determination that those events did not rise to the level of “persecution” is a fact-bound application of a general standard to a particular evidentiary record, and Congress’s review framework channels that kind of determination into substantial-evidence review rather than de novo reweighing. Nothing in § 1101(a)(42)(A) or § 1252’s judicial-review provisions singles out the persecution assessment for a different, less deferential mode of review, and respecting Congress’s allocation of decisional authority requires the court to affirm so long as the record does not compel the opposite conclusion. Under that deferential standard, the court of appeals properly upheld the agency because the evidence did not compel a finding of persecution notwithstanding the alleged threats and mistreatment.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The INA’s judicial-review framework directs courts of appeals to treat agency factfinding as conclusive unless “any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled” to reach the contrary conclusion, 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B), and the persecution inquiry here—whether the particular threats and physical mistreatment in this record were sufficiently severe—turns on an intensely fact-bound assessment of degree and context that is traditionally reviewed for substantial evidence. Parsing the statutory scheme, Congress did not provide a separate, nondeferential standard for this kind of record-specific application, and nothing in § 1101(a)(42)(A) converts the agency’s severity determination into a purely legal question when the governing legal definition of “persecution” is undisputed. Consistent with our approach in Patel to respecting Congress’s allocation of decisional responsibility in the INA’s review provisions, the court of appeals properly refrained from reweighing the evidence and instead asked only whether the agency’s no-persecution determination was supported by substantial evidence on these facts. De novo review remains available for genuine legal errors (e.g., misdefining persecution or applying an impermissible categorical rule), but petitioners’ challenge, as presented, seeks a more searching reappraisal of the record than § 1252(b)(4)(B) permits.
